Hays|United States of America.f: Buffalo Bill Cody co-founded the nearby town of Rome in 1867, but cholera and the railroad emptied it into Hays City within a year.

Mason City|United States of America.f: Mason City inspired River City in The Music Man and has the Park Inn, Frank Lloyd Wright's last remaining intact hotel.

Cape Girardeau|United States of America.f: The Cape in the name was a rock promontory over the Mississippi that was later destroyed by railroad construction.

Lake Charles|United States of America.f: Lake Charles ties with Port Arthur, Texas, and Astoria, Oregon, as the most humid city in the contiguous United States.

Macon|United States of America.f: Macon merged with Bibb County in 2014, becoming Georgia's fourth-largest city after Atlanta, Columbus and Augusta.

Muskegon|United States of America.f: The name Muskegon comes from the Ottawa word mashkiigong, meaning marshy river or swamp.

St. Paul Island|United States of America.f: Woolly mammoths lived on St. Paul Island until about 5,600 years ago, making it one of their last refuges.

Valdez|United States of America.f: A Spanish explorer named Valdez in 1790 for his navy minister, and today it is the terminus of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

Paducah|United States of America.f: Paducah was long said to honor a Chickasaw chief, but historians think William Clark named it for the Comanche, or Padoucas.

Escanaba|United States of America.f: Escanaba is an Ojibwe-derived name that roughly translates to land of the red buck, though some say it means flat rock.

New Bern|United States of America.f: Swiss and Palatine settlers founded New Bern in 1710 and named it for Bern, and it was North Carolina's capital from 1770 to 1792.

McCook|United States of America.f: McCook has the Sutton House, a Frank Lloyd Wright design built in 1907 and 1908.

Devils Lake|United States of America.f: Devils Lake comes from the Dakota mni wakan, meaning spirit water, which settlers misread as Bad Spirit Lake.

Ogdensburg|United States of America.f: Ogdensburg's port is the only U.S. port on the St. Lawrence Seaway.

Salisbury|United States of America.f: Salisbury is the headquarters of Perdue Farms, the poultry company that employs nearly 22,000 people.

Bethel|United States of America.f: In 2012 a prank flyer announced a Taco Bell in Bethel, so the chain airlifted in a food truck with ingredients for 10,000 tacos.

Dillingham|United States of America.f: Dillingham is the hub of Bristol Bay, which has the world's largest runs of wild sockeye salmon.

Petersburg|United States of America.f: Founded by Norwegian Peter Buschmann, Petersburg is nicknamed Little Norway, and early canneries cooled fish with LeConte Glacier ice.

Bradford|United States of America.f: The Taylor Cub was first built in Bradford, and after William Piper bought the firm it became the Piper Cub.

Nantucket|United States of America.f: Nantucket is nicknamed the Little Grey Lady of the Sea for how it looks from the water when fog-bound.

Pendleton|United States of America.f: Pendleton's old Chinatown is said to sit above a network of tunnels, now a tourist draw, though their origin is questioned.

Jackson (WY)|United States of America.f: Jackson elected an all-woman town government in 1920, including the mayor, council, marshal and clerk.

Kotzebue|United States of America.f: Kotzebue's Inupiaq name Qikiqtagruk means small island, and its English name honors Otto von Kotzebue, who explored the sound in 1818.

Jonesboro|United States of America.f: Jonesboro was named for state senator William A. Jones, who backed the 1859 creation of Craighead County.

Aniak|United States of America.f: Temperatures at Aniak on the Kuskokwim River range from -72 F in winter to 92 F in summer.

Nome|United States of America.f: The Iditarod ends in Nome, following the route of the 1925 dog sled relay that carried diphtheria serum, led by Balto and Togo.

Harrison|United States of America.f: A 1955 monument on Harrison's square honors victims of the 1857 Mountain Meadows massacre, whose wagon train assembled just south of town.

Burlington (IA)|United States of America.f: Burlington is home to Snake Alley, billed as the crookedest street on earth.

McCall|United States of America.f: Tom McCall founded the town in 1889 by trading a team of horses for a cabin and squatter rights to 160 acres on Payette Lake.

San Luis Obispo|United States of America.f: San Luis Obispo grew around a mission founded in 1772 on a Chumash site called tilhini, meaning place of the full moon.

Arcata|United States of America.f: The name Arcata comes from the Yurok oket'oh, meaning where there is a lagoon, a reference to Humboldt Bay.

Santa Barbara|United States of America.f: Santa Barbara sits on the longest south-facing stretch of coastline on the West Coast of the U.S. outside Alaska.

Fort Leonard Wood|United States of Ameri.f: The name Leonard Wood was briefly given to Maryland's Camp Meade in 1928 until Pennsylvania legislators got it changed back.

Trenton|United States of America.f: Trenton served as the capital of the United States from November 1 to December 24, 1784.

Kirksville|United States of America.f: Tradition says Jesse Kirk got the town named for him by sharing a dinner of turkey and whiskey with the surveyors.

Jackson (TN)|United States of America.f: Jackson was first called Alexandria, and was renamed in 1822 to honor Andrew Jackson, hero of the War of 1812.

Staunton|United States of America.f: Staunton served as Virginia's capital in June 1781, when legislators fled Richmond and Charlottesville to avoid British capture.

Santa Rosa|United States of America.f: Mexican colonists named Santa Rosa for Saint Rose of Lima, and it is now the largest city in California's Wine Country.

Galena|United States of America.f: Galena takes its name from the lead ore mines that opened nearby in 1918 and 1919.

Wrangell|United States of America.f: Wrangell is the only Alaskan city governed under four flags: Tlingit, Russian, British and American.
